slides.html: 1–2. Present Value and Bonds
slides.title: 1–2. Present Value and Bonds

slides.html:
Annuities and Perpetuities

Present value
annuity C\cdot\dfrac1r\Big[1-\dfrac1{(1+r)^T}\Big]
perpetuity C/r (100 at 10% ⟹ 1000)
growing perpetuity C/(r-g), r>g

Steps: match the compounding-period rate → timeline → sum → discount once more for each period of delay → solve
slides.title: Annuities and Perpetuities
A bond is a string of cash flows on a time line

slides.html:
A Bond Is the Present Value of Its Cash Flows

P=\sum\frac C{(1+r)^t}+\frac F{(1+r)^T}
  • coupon rate > discount rate ⟹ premium; < ⟹ discount; = ⟹ par
  • rates up, prices down; flight to safety bids bond prices up
  • two-year 10% semi-annual: 5%/half-year ⟹ 100; 4% ⟹ 103.63
slides.title: A Bond Is the Present Value of Its Cash Flows

slides.html:
YTM, Inflation, Holding-Period Return

  • YTM: the root of P=\sum C/(1+y)^t+F/(1+y)^T (Excel IRR)
  • Fisher: 1+\text{nominal}=(1+\text{real})(1+\text{inflation}); nominal 2.04% and inflation 6% ⟹ real -3.74\%
  • nominal flows at nominal rates, real flows at real rates — no separate inflation adjustment
  • holding-period return: V_{end}/V_{begin}-1 (with reinvestment)
  • NPV = 0 ≠ earning nothing: you earn the discount rate
slides.title: YTM, Inflation, Holding-Period Return

slides.html: 3–4. Term Structure and Duration
slides.title: 3–4. Term Structure and Duration

slides.html:
Spot and Forward Rates

1+s(n)=\big[(1+r_1)\cdots(1+r_n)\big]^{1/n},\qquad(1+f_{t_1,t_2})^{t_2-t_1}=\frac{(1+s(t_2))^{t_2}}{(1+s(t_1))^{t_1}}
  • short rates (8,10,11,11)\% ⟹ s=9.0,\ 9.66,\ 9.99\%
  • coupon bond = sum of zeros; spot rates can be extracted recursively
  • synthetic forward loan: buy a 1-year zero, short a 2-year zero, zero cash flow today
  • the YTM differs from every spot rate
slides.title: Spot and Forward Rates

slides.html:
Duration

D=\sum t\frac{PV(CF_t)}{P},\quad D^*=\frac D{1+y},\quad\frac{\Delta P}P\approx-D^*\Delta y
  • a zero's duration = its maturity; a coupon bond's duration < maturity
  • 30-year 8% bond: D=12.16, D^*=11.26
  • portfolio duration = weighted average of component durations
slides.title: Duration

slides.html:
Immunisation

  • banks: long-duration assets, short-duration liabilities ⟹ net worth falls when rates rise
  • immunise: asset duration = liability duration
  • GIC example: 5-year liability 14,693.28; a 6-year zero ⟹ shortfall 267.15 at 10%; a coupon bond with duration 4.99 nearly matches
  • pension example: 7-year liability, 3x+11(1-x)=7 ⟹ x=\tfrac12; a year later x=\tfrac59 — rebalance
slides.title: Immunisation

slides.html: 5. Stock Valuation
slides.title: 5. Stock Valuation

slides.html:
Dividend Discount and Gordon Models

P_0=\sum\frac{D_t}{(1+r)^t}\ \text{(no bubbles)},\qquad P_0=\frac{D_1}{r-g}
  • r=D_1/P_0+g: required return = dividend yield + capital gain
  • a non-paying firm still has a positive price: the market expects future dividends
  • multi-stage: the Webster example =71.70
slides.title: Dividend Discount and Gordon Models

slides.html:
Growth from Reinvestment: NPVGO

g=(1-\delta)R,\qquad P=\frac Er+\text{NPVGO}
  • R>r: retain everything; R=r: policy irrelevant; R<r: pay everything out
  • EPS 5, retain 40%, R=20\%, r=12\%: g=8\%, P=3/(0.12-0.08)=75
  • with R=10\%: g=4\%>0 but NPVGO =-4.17, P=37.50
  • growth ≠ value
slides.title: Growth from Reinvestment: NPVGO

slides.html:
The P/E Ratio

\frac PE=\frac1r+\frac{\text{NPVGO}}E
  • many growth opportunities ⟹ high P/E (Starbucks 50, Ford 7.69)
  • like a house's price–rent ratio
  • caveats: EPS is accounting, manipulable; no absolute standard of cheap or dear
  • the Gordon model's flaw: r is exogenous
slides.title: The P/E Ratio

slides.html: 6–7. Statistics and Portfolio Theory
slides.title: 6–7. Statistics and Portfolio Theory

slides.html:
Statistics

  • E[X], \mathrm{Var}, \mathrm{Cov}(X,Y), \rho=\mathrm{Cov}/(\sigma_X\sigma_Y)
  • best linear predictor: b=\mathrm{Cov}/\mathrm{Var}, minimum MSE \mathrm{Var}(Y)(1-\rho^2)
  • two two-state random variables always have correlation \pm1
  • Supertech: E=17.5\%, \sigma=25.9\%; Slowpoke: E=5.5\%, \sigma=11.5\%; \rho=-0.16
slides.title: Statistics

slides.html:
The Mean–Variance Frontier

minimise variance subject to \sum w_i=1, \sum w_iE[r_i]=m ⟹ variance is a quadratic in m ⟹ a hyperbola

  • three uncorrelated assets, variance 1, means 1,2,3: \mathrm{Var}=m^2-2m+\tfrac73
  • feasible set · frontier · efficient frontier (upper branch) · minimum-variance portfolio
slides.title: The Mean–Variance Frontier

slides.html: 8–9. CAPM and Efficient Markets
slides.title: 8–9. CAPM and Efficient Markets

slides.html:
Market Portfolio and the SML

  • homogeneous expectations ⟹ everyone holds the same risky portfolio = the market portfolio
  • CML: E(r_e)=r_f+\dfrac{E(r_m)-r_f}{\sigma_m}\sigma_e
  • \beta_i=\dfrac{\mathrm{Cov}(r_i,r_m)}{\mathrm{Var}(r_m)}; a portfolio's \beta is a weighted average

CAPM: E(r_i)=r_f+\beta_i[E(r_m)-r_f]. Only systematic risk is priced.
slides.title: Market Portfolio and the SML
The SML and Assessing the CAPM

slides.html:
Efficient Markets

A market is efficient with respect to an information set iff it is fully reflected in prices ⟹ no excess returns from it

  • Lenovo: dividends 1,2,1,2; price alternates 14.76,\ 15.24, return 10% each year ⟹ efficient; with prices 10,20,\dots ⟹ exploitable
  • prices react only to surprises (Apple's $8.8bn profit, price −5%)
  • weak ⊂ semi-strong ⊂ strong
slides.title: Efficient Markets

slides.html:
Evidence on Efficiency

  • weak form: random walk, tiny serial correlation
  • semi-strong: funds do not beat the market; event studies, AR and CAR
  • against: 19 October 1987; post-earnings drift
  • Grossman–Stiglitz: inefficient ⟹ search removes it; efficient ⟹ nobody searches
  • efficiency is a long-run tendency
slides.title: Evidence on Efficiency

slides.html: 10. Expected Utility and Risk Aversion
slides.title: 10. Expected Utility and Risk Aversion

slides.html:
Arrow–Pratt and Pratt's Theorem

A=-\frac{u''}{u'},\quad R=xA

A_1\ge A_2\iff\rho_1\ge\rho_2\iff u_1=f\circ u_2,\ f concave

  • CARA / IARA / DARA (evidence favours DARA)
  • CRRA u=\dfrac{x^{1-a}}{1-a} ⟹ DARA
  • double-or-halve gamble: p=0.5\Rightarrow a=1; 0.8\Rightarrow3; 0.99\Rightarrow7.6
slides.title: Arrow–Pratt and Pratt's Theorem

slides.html:
Demand for One Risky Asset

\max_aE[u(W_0R_f+(R-R_f)a)],\quad E[u'(W)(R-R_f)]=0
  • a^*>0\iff E[R]>R_f
  • DARA ⟹ normal good; IARA ⟹ inferior; CARA ⟹ independent of wealth
  • example: R_f=1.1, R=2/0.8: log a=11W_0/9; CARA a=\ln3/1.2
  • two-fund separation ⟺ u'=(A+By)^C or Ae^{By}
slides.title: Demand for One Risky Asset

slides.html:
Greater Risk

Rothschild–Stiglitz: Y-EY\overset d=X-EX+Z, E[Z|X]=0

  • equal means: Y riskier ⟺ every concave u prefers X ⟺ larger risk premium
  • greater risk ≠ greater variance (X=\{1,3,4,6\} versus Y); variance corresponds to quadratic utility
  • exception: for normals the two coincide
slides.title: Greater Risk

slides.html: 11. Consumption-Based Asset Pricing
slides.title: 11. Consumption-Based Asset Pricing

slides.html:
The Euler Equation and the SDF

p_iu'(c_0)=\beta E[u'(c_1)x_i]\ \Rightarrow\ \boxed{p=E[mx]},\quad m=\beta\frac{u'(c_1)}{u'(c_0)}
  • riskless bond: R_f=1/E[m] (where interest rates come from)
  • example: log utility, c_1=(3,1): m=(1/3,1), p_f=2/3; stock (4,-1): p=1/6
  • risk neutrality: m=\beta; no uncertainty: p=x/R_f
slides.title: The Euler Equation and the SDF

slides.html:
The Risk Correction

p=\frac{E[x]}{R_f}+\mathrm{Cov}(m,x)
  • payoff positively correlated with m (pays when "hungry"): valuable insurance, negative premium
  • negatively correlated: risky, positive premium
  • volatile ≠ risky: with \mathrm{Cov}=0 the price is E[x]/R_f
  • systematic risk is priced, idiosyncratic risk is not
slides.title: The Risk Correction

slides.html:
Determinants of the Rate, and Examples

CRRA + log-normal: r_f=-\ln\beta+a\mu-\tfrac12a^2\sigma^2

  • more patient, lower growth, more risk ⟹ lower rate
  • representative agent: no trade, c=e; prices are supported by the Euler equation
  • example: m=(1,1/3); U pays (0,2): p=1/3 (risky); V pays (2,0): p=1
slides.title: Determinants of the Rate, and Examples

slides.html:
Single-Beta Model and the Way Out

E[R_i]-R_f=\beta_{i,-m}\lambda_m,\quad\lambda_m=\frac{\mathrm{Var}(m)}{E[m]}
  • frontier returns are all perfectly negatively correlated with m; the CAPM is a special case
  • directions: the Allais paradox and new preferences, better consumption data, heterogeneity, incomplete markets, learning, rare disasters
slides.title: Single-Beta Model and the Way Out

slides.html: 12. No Arbitrage and Risk-Neutral Pricing
slides.title: 12. No Arbitrage and Risk-Neutral Pricing

slides.html:
Risk-Neutral Probabilities

\pi^*(s)=\frac{p(c(s))}{\sum p(c(s'))},\qquad p(x)=\frac{E^*[x]}{R_f}
  • example: u=-e^{-x}, endowment (2,3): \pi^*=(0.73,0.27), R_f=3.97; an asset paying (2,1) costs 0.44
  • in the risk-neutral world every asset earns the riskless return
slides.title: Risk-Neutral Probabilities

slides.html:
The Law of One Price and No Arbitrage

  • LOOP ⟺ an SDF exists (no completeness, no equilibrium needed)
  • no arbitrage ⟺ a strictly positive SDF exists
  • arbitrage: hX\ge0, ph\le0, one strict; strong arbitrage is a special case
  • no arbitrage ⟹ LOOP, not conversely
slides.title: The Law of One Price and No Arbitrage

slides.html:
Violations and Limits to Arbitrage

  • country-fund premia (Taiwan Fund 207%), ADRs, Royal Dutch Shell (ratio 1.5), Palm/3Com (negative stub)
  • limits: short-sale constraints, institutional constraints, risk — violations are mostly risky bets
  • LTCM's Royal Dutch/Shell pairs trade (1998)
slides.title: Violations and Limits to Arbitrage

slides.html: 13. Options
slides.title: 13. Options

slides.html:
Put–Call Parity and Bounds

C+PV(X)=P+S\qquad(\text{with dividends: }+PV(D))
  • example: 8-2+40/1.1=42.36
  • no dividends: an American call is never exercised early; an American put may be
  • \max(S-PV(X),0)\le C\le S
  • effects of volatility, maturity, rate, strike and underlying price
slides.title: Put–Call Parity and Bounds

slides.html:
Replication and the Binomial Tree

Stock 50 → 60 / 40, R=1.1, strike 50: buy \tfrac12 share, borrow 18.18 ⟹ C=25-18.18=6.82

C=\frac1R[qC_u+(1-q)C_d],\quad q=\frac{R-d}{u-d},\quad u>R>d
  • q: the risk-neutral probability, the stock's expected return =R
  • the natural probability p is not used — but it is embedded in u,d,R
slides.title: Replication and the Binomial Tree

slides.html:
The Link to the SDF

representative consumer e_1=(1,2), log: m=(1,\tfrac12), state prices (\tfrac12,\tfrac14)

  • R=\tfrac43, u=\tfrac83, d=\tfrac23, q=\tfrac13=\pi^*(s_2); call =\tfrac12
  • natural probabilities to (\tfrac23,\tfrac13): R'=\tfrac65, q'=\tfrac15, C'=\tfrac13 — it changes
  • absolute pricing (equilibrium) vs relative pricing (binomial)
slides.title: The Link to the SDF

slides.html: 14. Forwards, Futures and Swaps
slides.title: 14. Forwards, Futures and Swaps

slides.html:
The Forward Price

F_{t,T}=S_t(1+r)^{T-t}
  • zero value at inception; payoff S_T-F_{0,T} at maturity
  • arbitrage proof: borrow, buy the asset, short a forward
  • storage / income: F=S(1+r)^T+\mathrm{FV}(c); convenience yield: F=(S+U)e^{(r-y)T}
  • value f_{0,t}=S_t-F_{0,T}/(1+r)^{T-t}; example: 25-24e^{-0.05}=2.17
slides.title: The Forward Price

slides.html:
Futures and Hedging

  • futures: standardised, clearinghouse, daily marking to market, margin and maintenance margin
  • with deterministic rates futures price = forward price
  • long hedge: soybeans at 0.33 locks cost; short hedge: sell USD futures, locks 6.8 CNY/USD
  • leverage: margin 9.9, price +1 ⟹ 10.1% return (spot 1.02%)
  • Barings, Showa Shell; airlines: options are safer than futures
slides.title: Futures and Hedging

slides.html:
Swaps

  • interest-rate swap: fixed for floating; zero value at inception
  • currency swap: a 6% dollar debt ⟹ a 5% euro debt
  • CDS: the buyer pays a spread, receives face value on default; naked CDS
  • 2007–2008: CDOs, rating agencies underestimated risk, AIG exposure over $100 billion
slides.title: Swaps

slides.html: 15–16. Corporate Debt and Capital Structure
slides.title: 15–16. Corporate Debt and Capital Structure

slides.html:
MM Proposition I (No Taxes)

V_L=V_U: capital structure does not affect firm value or the share price.

  • A (no debt) vs B (debt 5): V=10; if B's equity were worth 6 ⟹ homemade-leverage arbitrage
  • assumptions: symmetric information, equal borrowing rates, no taxes, no arbitrage, no bankruptcy costs
  • r_{WACC}=r_0, \beta_0=\beta_{WACC}
slides.title: MM Proposition I (No Taxes)

slides.html:
With Taxes: the Tax Shield

V_L=V_U+t_cD,\quad r_e=r_0+(r_0-r_d)(1-t_c)\frac DE,\quad r_{WACC}=r_0\Big(1-t_c\frac DV\Big)
  • EBIT 1 million, debt 4 million: tax shield =0.35\times400{,}000=140{,}000
  • Divided Airlines: V_L=570, share price 5.7, r_e=25.27\%, r_{WACC}=17.54\%
slides.title: With Taxes: the Tax Shield

slides.html:
The Pecking Order and the Evidence

  • asymmetric information: internal funds first, then debt, equity last; no target ratio
  • 392 CFOs: 81% have a target debt ratio
  • industry differences: airlines 59.7%, software 2.3%
  • Rajan–Zingales: size and tangibles ↑; profitability and market-to-book ↓
  • no single theory explains everything
slides.title: The Pecking Order and the Evidence

A Map of Methods

Problem Method
money at different dates present value, compounding
rate sensitivity duration, convexity, immunisation
stock value DDM, NPVGO
risk and return mean–variance, CAPM
how risk is priced SDF, Euler equation, no arbitrage

slides.title: A Map of Methods

slides.html:
Threads Through the Text

  1. price = expectation of future payoff × stochastic discount factor
  2. only systematic risk is priced
  3. no arbitrage: price derivatives without knowing risk preferences
  4. a good model identifies key elements, shows how they relate and fits the evidence — the equity premium puzzle shows where we fall short
slides.title: Threads Through the Text

slides.html:
Common misconceptions

Misconception Correct
Add money from different years directly Discount to a common date first
A volatile asset must earn more Only systematic risk is rewarded
Beta measures total risk Sensitivity to the market only
Option prices depend on the chance of a rise Set by replication cost
The forward price forecasts the spot price Set by cost of carry
More debt is always cheaper MM: irrelevant without frictions; with taxes a trade-off
slides.title: Common misconceptions
